title: Frontcountry and Backcountry Lightning Risk Management (NWS/NOLS brochure)
claims: Backcountry settings are at least a 30-minute walk from the nearest vehicles or modern buildings; four ranked actions reduce risk, each roughly twice as important as the next: time visits with local weather; find safer terrain when hearing thunder; avoid trees and long conductors once lightning gets close; take the lightning position if striking nearby and unable to move.

Ground current contributes to about half of lightning fatalities; keep feet close together and avoid lying flat. Side flash jumps from tall objects, so do not shelter near tall trees or tall vertical surfaces; contact injury comes from touching long conductors such as railings, cables and fences; direct strikes cause about 3-5% of fatalities.

Begin turnaround when you hear thunder, which means lightning is less than 10 miles away; avoid peaks, ridges and significantly higher ground; if possible, descend on the side without cloud cover, and move to safer terrain as soon as you hear thunder.

Spread the group at 20-foot (7 m) intervals to reduce multiple injuries; the lightning position keeps feet together and reduces the ground footprint, while lying flat increases ground-current exposure.
Avoid cave entrances and small overhangs because arcs can cross the gap; stay out of water and away from metal conductors such as ladders, cables and railings.
In first aid, triage reverses the usual order: attend first to those in cardiac or respiratory arrest without obvious lethal injury; lightning victims do not carry a residual charge.
